subject: Business
title: Sustainability in Supply Chains
description: A micro-lesson that makes Sustainability in Supply Chains usable.

hook.text: A pair of jeans uses 7,500 liters of water to produce. Most of that water use is invisible to the buyer.

buildup.text: Supply chains account for over 80% of most companies' total carbon emissions — far more than offices or factories.

discovery.text: Scope 3 emissions (supply chain) are the hardest to measure and the largest category for most businesses.

twist.text: Consumers demand sustainability, but few will pay more. The cost pressure falls entirely on the supply chain.

climax.text: IKEA aims for a fully circular supply chain by 2030: every product designed for reuse, repair, or recycling.

punchline.text: The greenest supply chain isn't the one that offsets. It's the one that wastes nothing.

quiz.question: What percentage of a company's carbon emissions typically come from its supply chain?

details.summary: Sustainable supply chain management integrates environmental and social considerations into sourcing, production, logistics, and end-of-life management. It encompasses carbon footprint reduction, circular economy principles, and compliance with growing environmental regulations.
details.whyItMatters: Supply chains account for over 80 percent of most companies' total carbon emissions. Addressing Scope 3 emissions through sustainable supply chain practices is essential for meeting climate commitments and satisfying investor ESG expectations.
takeaways: Supply chains generate over 80% of most companies' total carbon emissions
Circular economy designs products for reuse, repair, and recycling
Scope 3 emissions reporting drives supplier sustainability requirements

faq.question: What are Scope 3 emissions and why do they matter for supply chains?
faq.answer: Scope 3 covers indirect emissions from a company's entire value chain including purchased goods, transportation, and product use. They typically account for 80-90% of total emissions. Reporting frameworks increasingly require measuring and reducing Scope 3.

faq.question: How does the circular economy concept apply to supply chains?
faq.answer: Instead of linear take-make-dispose flows, circular supply chains design products for durability, reuse, and recyclability. Reverse logistics recovers used products and materials. Remanufacturing restores products to like-new condition, reducing waste and resource consumption.
